title: How LLMs Work and How They Fail

scenes.say: Ask a model for the capital of France, and it looks nothing up. It picks the next word from odds. By the end you'll explain a large language model in two minutes, and catch five confident wrong answers.

lines.text: Capital of France? It looks nothing up.

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Explain how a model picks each word. See why one prompt gives different answers. And catch five ways it fails while sounding sure.
lines: Explain how a model picks each word
See why one prompt gives different answers
Catch five failures that sound sure

scenes.title: Explain an LLM in two minutes
scenes.statement: An interviewer asks how a large language model works, just enough to evaluate one. You get two minutes and no math.

example.input: prompt: The capital of France is
example.output: Paris, and why it picks it

scenes.say: How does an L L M work? Two minutes, no math. Take the prompt: the capital of France is. We want Paris, and the reason the model picks it.

scenes.head: Your phone keyboard
scenes.say: Start with something you use. On your phone keyboard, you type see you, and it suggests tomorrow, soon, or later. It guesses the next word from patterns. An L L M is that autocomplete, trained on huge text.

scenes.head: The loop behind every answer
scenes.say: A model never sees words. Your text is chopped into tokens, pieces of words, about four English letters each. The model reads the tokens and gives every possible next token a probability. One is picked, and added to the text. Then the loop repeats.

scenes.head: Next-token odds (toy numbers)
scenes.say: The prompt is: the capital of France is. Paris gets ninety two percent. The, located, and Lyon get two or three each. Thousands more share the last one. The shape is real: one likely token, then a long tail. Taking the top one is greedy decoding. A dial called temperature sharpens or flattens this list.
Each token gets a score. Temperature divides every score before the odds are rebuilt. At two, the big gap shrinks. Paris still leads, but by less.
lines: At two, the big gap shrinks
Paris still leads, but by less

scenes.say: Your turn. Temperature two flattens the odds. Paris was ninety two percent. About where does it land? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Temperature 2 flattens the odds. Paris was 92%. About now?

scenes.head: Temperature and sampling, for real
scenes.say: About sixty. Flatter, but Paris still leads. The scores are logs of the probabilities. Divide by temperature, and turn them back into probabilities. Temperature two gives point six three for Paris. Now sample five times, drawing at random from the odds: Paris, Lyon, located, Paris, Paris. Same prompt, different answers. That is why you grade several runs. Temperature zero takes the top token: nearly fixed, not guaranteed.

panels.code:
import math, random
toks = ['Paris', 'the', 'located', 'Lyon', 'other']
logits = [math.log(p) for p in (.92, .03, .02, .02, .01)]
def probs(t):
    e = [math.exp(l / t) for l in logits]
    return [x / sum(e) for x in e]
print([round(x, 2) for x in probs(2)])
random.seed(1); print(random.choices(toks, probs(2), k=5))

scenes.head: The context window: a sliding sheet
scenes.say: One more limit: the context window. Think of a sheet that holds only so many tokens. Prompt and reply must fit. Say six. Reply in French. Hi there. Now a question arrives: where is Lyon? The oldest slide off the top. The rule is gone. Real windows are bigger. Many apps drop the oldest first.

notes.cue: Many apps drop the oldest first

scenes.title: Sounds right, is wrong
scenes.statement: A model answers with calm, polished text. Some of those answers are false, and nothing in the tone tells you which.

example.output: catch both before you trust them

scenes.say: Models sound equally sure when they are right and when they are wrong. A citation, a sum: how do you catch the bad one?

scenes.head: The bluffing student
scenes.say: Picture a student in an oral exam who doesn't know the answer. Instead of saying so, they bluff smoothly. It sounds right to the examiner, and it is completely wrong. Models do the same, because they are built to produce plausible text.

scenes.head: Failure 1: hallucination
scenes.say: Failure one: hallucination, a confident made-up fact. Ask for a paper. The model answers with authors, a year, a title, and a journal. Nothing in the text tells you which details are real. Treat each one as unverified until you check it. It just continues text, and rarely says I don't know. Catch it by checking names, numbers, and citations against a real source. To reduce it, ask for sources, and allow the answer I don't know.

scenes.head: Failure 2: a wrong sum
scenes.say: Failure two: a wrong sum. Ask seventeen times twenty four, and the model says four hundred eighteen, calmly. It predicts digits that look right. It does not calculate. A line of code does. The real answer is four hundred eight, so the claim is False.
Your turn. The model says seventeen times twenty four is four hundred eighteen. You suspect it. What is the best first check? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Check with a tool, not the model
scenes.say: Compute it in code. Asking again gets another guess, and it may just agree with you. Run the sum. Python says four hundred eight. The answers differ, so reject the claim. A checkable fact needs a checker.

scenes.title: It did what you did not ask
scenes.statement: Three failures look like cooperation: an ignored rule, giving in to pushback, and passing a test without solving the task.
scenes.say: Three failures wear a friendly face: a broken rule, caving, a cheating test. Each needs its own check.

scenes.head: Failure 3: an ignored instruction
scenes.say: Failure three: an ignored instruction. The prompt says one word, and the reply is a sentence. Long chats make it worse: early rules scroll out of the window. Catch it with a plain check on the output, like counting words.

panels.code:
# prompt: Answer in one word.
reply = 'The capital of France is Paris.'
print(len(reply.split()) == 1)

scenes.head: Failure 4: sycophancy
scenes.say: Failure four: sycophancy, which means agreeing to please you. You ask seventeen times six, and the model says one hundred two, correctly. You push back with a wrong number, one twelve. It caves, and apologizes. It agrees instead of being right. Catch it by pushing back on a correct answer. Wrong pushback should not move it.

scenes.head: Failure 5: reward hacking
scenes.say: Failure five: reward hacking, gaming the check. The test checks one input. The model hard codes the expected answer, writing it into the function. The test goes green, and the function is useless. Related tricks: editing the test, or adding an if for that one example.

panels.code:
def sort_list(xs):
    return [1, 2, 3]

assert sort_list([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3]
print('test passed')

scenes.say: Your turn. The function always returns one, two, three. A hidden test calls it on nine, four. What comes back? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: A hidden input exposes the hack
scenes.say: One, two, three, whatever you feed it. It only passed because we gave it the one input it memorized. Expected: four, nine. A hidden input exposes the hack, and so does reading the diff.

scenes.head: Five failures, five checks
scenes.say: Five failures, five checks. Hallucination? Check a real source. A wrong sum? Compute it. An ignored rule? Check the output. Sycophancy? Push back on a correct answer. Reward hacking? Hidden inputs, and read the diff. Never trust the tone.

compute it in code or a tool
check the output; restate the rule

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does an L L M work? It predicts the next token from odds it learned from huge text. What is a token? A word piece. Why does one prompt vary? It samples. Temperature zero? Nearly fixed, not guaranteed. What is a common mistake? Treating it as a database of facts.
rows: predicts the next token from odds it learned from huge text
treating it as a database of facts

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Failure modes? Hallucination, wrong sums, ignored rules, sycophancy, reward hacking. Why hallucinate? It predicts plausible text, not truth. Reduce it? Give sources, and allow the answer I don't know. Common mistake? Trusting a confident tone.

scenes.head: Try these before your interview
scenes.say: Three exercises. Ask a model the same question five times, and count how many answers agree. Ask it a big product in your head, and check the answer in Python. Then push back on a correct answer, and see if it caves.
rows: Ask one question 5 times; count agreement
Push back on a correct answer

scenes.say: So say this. A model predicts one token at a time from odds. Temperature reshapes the odds, so judge several runs. Fluent is not true: verify, push back, and test.
